statement: Everyone at a meeting shakes hands with everyone else exactly once. There are 66 handshakes in total. How many people are there?

choices.misconception: I used the number of hands each person shakes rather than the number of people.
I doubled the answer, forgetting that the halving has already been done.
I halved 66 and treated that as the number of people.
I gave the number of handshakes back as the number of people.

hints: Work out the handshakes for a few small groups and write the results in a list. The pattern that appears lets you climb to 66 without any algebra.
3 people give 3 handshakes, 4 give 6, 5 give 10. The counts are 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55, 66 - and 66 is reached at 12 people.

solutions.reliable: Try small cases and list the results. With 3 people there are 3 handshakes, with 4 there are 6, with 5 there are 10. Continuing: 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55, 66. Counting along, 66 handshakes happens with 12 people. Check: each of 12 shakes 11 hands, giving 132 ends, and each handshake has two ends: 66. The transferable idea: small cases turn a question you cannot start into a list you can read the answer off.
solutions.elegant: n people give n(n - 1)/2 handshakes, so n(n - 1) = 132 = 12 x 11, giving n = 12.

whyOnTest: Starting small is the single most reliable way into a question that looks like it needs algebra a student has not met yet.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
